name: Ethics & Critical Thinking
description: An elective course introducing students to moral philosophy, logical reasoning, and applied ethics, developing skills for rigorous ethical analysis of real-world issues.

modules.title: Introduction to Ethics & Moral Philosophy
modules.titleZh: 伦理学与道德哲学导论
modules.objectives: Define ethics and distinguish it from law, religion, and social convention; explain why ethical reasoning matters in personal and public life.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Business Ethics §1.1 — ethical reasoning, integrity, and the difference between legal compliance and ethical responsibility.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Introduction to Ethics & Moral Philosophy; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — apply the distinction between what is legal, profitable, and ethically justified.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: A fictional school proposes face-recognition attendance. The packet says it may reduce check-in time by four minutes, state law permits it with notice, 62% of families support it, and the vendor retains face templates for three years. Task: Write 450–550 words that separate one legal claim, one social-convention claim, and two ethical claims. Identify stakeholders, distinguish facts from value judgments, and defend a policy recommendation without assuming that legal means ethical. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: category distinctions 25%; stakeholder/evidence analysis 30%; ethical reasoning 30%; organization 15%.

modules.title: Consequentialism & Utilitarianism
modules.objectives: Explain consequentialism and utilitarian ethics; apply the greatest happiness principle to real ethical dilemmas; evaluate strengths and weaknesses of consequentialist reasoning.
modules.readingNote: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — overview of consequentialist theories and objections.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Consequentialism & Utilitarianism; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — worked introduction to utilitarian cost-benefit reasoning.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: A relief committee has 100 supply units. Plan A helps 80 residents by 1 well-being point each; Plan B helps 30 residents by 3 points each; Plan C helps 60 residents by 1 point but imposes a 20-point loss on one resident. Treat the figures as fictional utilities for comparison only. Task: Calculate total net utility for all three plans, select the act-utilitarian choice, then write 400–500 words presenting a rights-based objection and explaining whether a rule-utilitarian could answer it. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: calculations 25%; correct utilitarian application 30%; objection and reply 30%; clarity 15%.

modules.title: Deontological Ethics (Kant)
modules.objectives: Explain Kant's categorical imperative and duty-based ethics; apply deontological reasoning to ethical cases; contrast deontology with consequentialism. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Kantian duty, maxims, universal law, and humanity.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Deontological Ethics (Kant); introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — practice distinguishing duties from outcome-based reasoning.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: A student promised a teammate not to show anyone the teammate's draft. The student later notices that one paragraph matches a publicly available article word for word. A teacher asks the student to provide any relevant evidence, including the draft, during an academic-integrity review. Task: Write 450–550 words. State the proposed maxim for each available response, test each under universal law, apply the Formula of Humanity to the teammate, teacher, author, and student, distinguish a valid promise from an apparent duty conflict, and defend a conclusion without relying only on consequences. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied facts, and reasoning that connects the facts to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: maxim/universal-law analysis 30%; humanity analysis 30%; promise/duty reasoning 25%; clarity 15%.

modules.title: Virtue Ethics (Aristotle)
modules.titleZh: 美德伦理学（亚里士多德）
modules.objectives: Explain Aristotle's virtue ethics and the concept of eudaimonia; identify the virtues and the doctrine of the mean; evaluate virtue ethics against other frameworks.
modules.readingNote: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Aristotle on virtue, practical wisdom, and flourishing.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Virtue Ethics (Aristotle); introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — apply virtue and character analysis to a case.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: Fictional team captain Mara admits her own scoring error, gives a nervous player a second attempt, refuses an unfair shortcut, and later ignores useful feedback because she fears looking uncertain. Task: Create a virtue table with four traits, the relevant excess and deficiency, and evidence from the profile. Then write 350–450 words explaining how practical wisdom could improve Mara's final choice and how flourishing differs from a single good outcome. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: virtue table 30%; evidence use 25%; practical-wisdom analysis 30%; organization 15%.

modules.title: Moral Relativism vs. Universalism
modules.titleZh: 道德相对主义与普遍主义
modules.objectives: Distinguish moral relativism from moral universalism; evaluate the philosophical arguments for each position; apply the debate to cross-cultural ethical cases.
modules.readingNote: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — arguments about moral relativism and disagreement.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Moral Relativism vs. Universalism; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: United Nations — primary text for evaluating a universal-rights claim.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: In fictional Coastland, a coming-of-age ceremony requires 16-year-olds to leave school for six months. Supporters cite tradition and belonging; critics report unequal consent and lasting educational loss. A rights charter protects culture, education, bodily autonomy, and equal treatment. Task: Write 500–600 words presenting the strongest relativist and universalist arguments. Distinguish understanding a practice from endorsing it, apply at least two charter rights, and defend a culturally respectful decision standard. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: fair presentation of both views 30%; rights/evidence application 30%; defended standard 25%; conventions 15%.

modules.title: Logic & Argument Structure
modules.objectives: Identify the components of a logical argument (premises, conclusion); distinguish deductive from inductive arguments; evaluate argument validity and soundness.
modules.readingNote: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy — validity, soundness, and counterexamples.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Logic & Argument Structure; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy — validity, soundness, and counterexamples in deductive arguments.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: Four arguments are supplied: (1) If the archive is complete, every listed file is searchable; the archive is complete; therefore every listed file is searchable. (2) If rain caused the outage, roads are wet; roads are wet; therefore rain caused the outage. (3) 18 of 20 sampled buses were on time; therefore most buses on this route are usually on time. (4) No verified report shows contamination; therefore contamination is impossible. Task: Rewrite each in premise-conclusion form, classify it as deductive or inductive, test validity/strength, and state what additional evidence would be needed. Include one counterexample for each invalid deductive form. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: standard form 25%; classification 20%; validity/strength analysis 35%; counterexamples/evidence 20%.

modules.title: Identifying Logical Fallacies
modules.objectives: Identify and explain common informal logical fallacies; recognize fallacious reasoning in everyday arguments and media. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Purdue OWL — definitions and examples of common informal fallacies.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Identifying Logical Fallacies; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Thou Shalt Not Commit Logical Fallacies — concise practice examples for classification and revision.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: Five fictional claims are supplied: 'Do not trust Lina's budget because she is lazy'; 'Kai wants later school start, so he wants students to sleep all day'; 'We added tutoring and scores rose, so tutoring caused every gain'; 'Either ban phones entirely or learning will disappear'; 'Thousands shared the post, so it must be true.' Task: Name the fallacy in each claim, explain the reasoning error in 2–3 sentences, and rewrite each as a fair, testable argument that would require relevant evidence. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied evidence or data, and reasoning that connects the evidence to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: correct classification 30%; explanations 30%; repaired arguments 30%; clarity 10%.

modules.title: Evaluating Evidence & Claims
modules.objectives: Apply criteria for evaluating evidence quality; distinguish strong from weak evidence types; identify bias in sources and arguments.
modules.readingNote: Mike Caulfield — the SIFT method for checking source reputation, coverage, and original context.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Evaluating Evidence & Claims; introduces the concepts and models used in the assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Digital Inquiry Group — civic online reasoning curriculum for lateral reading and source verification.
modules.assignment: Provided materials: Three fictional source cards address whether a tutoring program improved scores. Source A is a randomized study of 600 students with 8% attrition, funded by a public research office; it links its methods, preregistration, comparison-group results, and uncertainty interval. Source B is a news story quoting only the program director; its publisher accepts program advertising and it links no study or dataset. Source C is one family testimonial sponsored by the vendor; the speaker is named, but the original score record and comparison data are unavailable. All three report improvement. Task: Build an evidence-quality matrix covering method, sample, comparison, funding, traceability, and uncertainty. Then write 400–500 words stating what can and cannot be concluded and how SIFT checks would change confidence. Submit: one PDF or document with clearly labeled sections. Include: all requested work, the supplied facts, and reasoning that connects the facts to each conclusion. Do not contact real people, collect personal or health data, spend money, prescribe treatment, or use an unavailable source. Evaluation: matrix accuracy 30%; source comparison 25%; bounded conclusion 30%; organization 15%.

quizQuestions.question: Ethics is best defined as the branch of philosophy that:
options: Establishes the laws governments must follow
Determines religious rules for moral conduct
Studies moral principles about what is right, wrong, good, and bad
Describes how people actually behave in society
quizQuestions.answer: Studies moral principles about what is right, wrong, good, and bad
quizQuestions.explanation: Ethics (or moral philosophy) is the philosophical discipline that investigates principles for evaluating actions, character, and outcomes as right, wrong, good, or bad.

quizQuestions.question: An ethical argument differs from a legal argument in that an ethical argument:
options: Can only be made by trained philosophers and ethicists
Always reaches the same conclusion as legal analysis
Is based exclusively on religious texts and traditions
Addresses what is morally right or wrong, not merely what is legally permitted
quizQuestions.answer: Addresses what is morally right or wrong, not merely what is legally permitted
quizQuestions.explanation: Legal arguments focus on what statutes and courts permit; ethical arguments ask what is morally right, which may differ — slavery was once legal but is universally condemned as unethical.

quizQuestions.question: A city ordinance permits a data practice, but residents question whether it is fair. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Ethical evaluation can still examine harms, rights, and fairness
Legality settles every ethical question
Public approval automatically makes it ethical
Only religious rules can evaluate it
quizQuestions.answer: Ethical evaluation can still examine harms, rights, and fairness
quizQuestions.explanation: Law establishes enforceable rules, while ethical reasoning can still test whether a permitted practice respects rights, consequences, and fairness.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: The study of ethics matters in everyday life primarily because.
quizQuestions.answer: The study of ethics matters in everyday life because it helps people reason carefully about right and wrong, responsibilities, consequences, fairness, and the effects of their choices on others.
quizQuestions.explanation: A strong answer connects ethics to ordinary decision-making, not only abstract philosophy.

quizQuestions.question: The core principle of utilitarianism, as formulated by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, is:
options: Act as a person of good character would act in this situation
Act according to your duty regardless of consequences
Act to maximize overall happiness or well-being for the greatest number
Act according to principles that could be universal laws
quizQuestions.answer: Act to maximize overall happiness or well-being for the greatest number
quizQuestions.explanation: Utilitarianism's greatest happiness principle holds that the right action is the one that produces the greatest total happiness (pleasure, well-being) for the greatest number of people affected.

quizQuestions.question: The trolley problem is most commonly used in ethics to:
options: Demonstrate that all ethical dilemmas have clear correct answers
Show that consequentialism and deontology always reach the same conclusions
Teach students about the history of railway safety regulations
Explore the tension between utilitarian reasoning and deontological restrictions on harming individuals
quizQuestions.answer: Explore the tension between utilitarian reasoning and deontological restrictions on harming individuals
quizQuestions.explanation: Trolley cases compare outcome-focused reasoning with constraints on harming. In a switch case, the one person’s death may be a foreseen side effect; in a footbridge case, using a person’s body as the means creates a different deontological concern.

quizQuestions.question: The strongest objection to utilitarianism is that it can justify:
options: Violating individual rights to produce a better collective outcome
Making moral decisions too difficult by requiring calculation
Giving too much weight to individual rights and autonomy
Requiring perfect knowledge of all consequences before acting
quizQuestions.answer: Violating individual rights to produce a better collective outcome
quizQuestions.explanation: The most powerful objection to utilitarianism is that it can theoretically justify violating individual rights (e.g., torturing an innocent person) if doing so produces greater overall happiness.

quizQuestions.question: Two policies produce the same total benefit, but one concentrates a severe loss on a single person. This case most directly tests utilitarianism's treatment of:
options: Legal precedent
Deductive validity
Individual rights and distribution
Cultural description
quizQuestions.answer: Individual rights and distribution
quizQuestions.explanation: Aggregate utility can obscure who receives benefits and burdens, which motivates rights and justice objections.

quizQuestions.question: Immanuel Kant's categorical imperative is 'categorical' because it:
options: Applies only to specific categories of actions
Is based on cultural categories that vary across societies
Is derived from the consequences that different actions produce
Applies unconditionally regardless of consequences or desires
quizQuestions.answer: Applies unconditionally regardless of consequences or desires
quizQuestions.explanation: Kant's categorical imperative is unconditional — it applies to all rational beings in all circumstances, regardless of desired outcomes or contingent circumstances.

quizQuestions.question: Kant's Formula of Universal Law states that you should act only according to a maxim that:
options: Conforms to the traditions and customs of your society
You could will to become a universal law for all rational beings
Produces the best consequences for the greatest number
Reflects the virtuous character of an admirable person
quizQuestions.answer: You could will to become a universal law for all rational beings
quizQuestions.explanation: The Formula of Universal Law: 'Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.' If universalizing the rule leads to contradiction, the action is wrong.

quizQuestions.question: Kant's Formula of Humanity requires that you:
options: Act to maximize human happiness across all cultures
Always treat humanity — in yourself and others — as an end, never merely as a means
Follow the moral rules established by human governments
Act in the way that reflects human nature and natural law
quizQuestions.answer: Always treat humanity — in yourself and others — as an end, never merely as a means
quizQuestions.explanation: The Formula of Humanity holds that rational beings have inherent dignity and must never be used merely as tools for another person's ends — they must always be treated as ends in themselves.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Complete this statement: The main criticism of kantian ethics is that its absolute rules can...
quizQuestions.answer: A main criticism of Kantian ethics is that absolute duties can be too rigid when rules conflict or when following a rule would lead to serious harm.
quizQuestions.explanation: Kantian ethics emphasizes duty and universal principles, so critics often question whether it handles context, consequences, and competing obligations well enough.

quizQuestions.question: Aristotle's concept of eudaimonia is best translated as:
options: The avoidance of all pain and suffering
Human flourishing and the excellent exercise of our distinctively human capacities
Following the commands of the gods or divine law
Pleasure and sensory satisfaction
quizQuestions.answer: Human flourishing and the excellent exercise of our distinctively human capacities
quizQuestions.explanation: Eudaimonia is typically translated as 'flourishing' or 'happiness' — but it means living well by excellently exercising the rational capacities that are distinctive to humans.

quizQuestions.question: The 'doctrine of the mean' in Aristotle's virtue ethics holds that virtues are:
options: Absolute rules that should be followed regardless of context
Dispositions to respond appropriately to a situation, avoiding deficiency and excess
Socially determined by the community's traditions and norms
Behaviors exactly halfway between two extremes in all cases
quizQuestions.answer: Dispositions to respond appropriately to a situation, avoiding deficiency and excess
quizQuestions.explanation: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean holds that virtues are the appropriate middle ground between deficiency and excess — courage lies between cowardice and recklessness.

quizQuestions.question: In Aristotle's virtue ethics, moral character develops through:
options: Habitual practice and repeated performance of virtuous actions until they become second nature
Following the commands of moral authority figures
Studying philosophical texts about virtuous behavior
Calculating which actions produce the most beneficial consequences
quizQuestions.answer: Habitual practice and repeated performance of virtuous actions until they become second nature
quizQuestions.explanation: Aristotle held that virtues are not innate but are developed through habituation — repeated performance of virtuous actions gradually shapes a person's character and dispositions.

quizQuestions.question: Virtue ethics asks primarily which of the following question?
options: What kind of person should I be?
What duty am I obligated to perform?
What does my society's tradition require of me?
What action produces the best consequences?
quizQuestions.answer: What kind of person should I be?
quizQuestions.explanation: Virtue ethics focuses on character rather than rules or consequences — the central question is 'What kind of person should I be and what would a person of good character do?'

quizQuestions.question: Moral relativism is the view that:
options: All moral claims are false and there are no moral truths
Moral questions are always complex and rarely have clear answers
Moral standards vary across cultures and individuals and there are no universal moral truths
Morality is relative to consequences and nothing else
quizQuestions.answer: Moral standards vary across cultures and individuals and there are no universal moral truths
quizQuestions.explanation: Moral relativism holds that what is morally right or wrong is relative to the culture, society, or individual — there are no objective, universal moral standards.

quizQuestions.question: Moral universalism (moral objectivism) holds that:
options: Morality is whatever the majority of people in a society agree on
Universal morality is discovered through religious revelation alone
Some moral standards apply to all people in all cultures regardless of local customs
All cultures spontaneously arrive at the same moral conclusions
quizQuestions.answer: Some moral standards apply to all people in all cultures regardless of local customs
quizQuestions.explanation: Moral universalism holds that there are objective moral truths that apply to all humans regardless of cultural background, tradition, or individual preference.

quizQuestions.question: The fact that cultures disagree about a practice logically proves which conclusion?
options: That the majority culture is correct
That no universal principle is possible
Only that moral disagreement exists
That every practice is equally justified
quizQuestions.answer: Only that moral disagreement exists
quizQuestions.explanation: Disagreement is evidence of variation, but by itself it does not establish that no position can be better justified.

quizQuestions.question: A universalist position is strongest when it:
options: Applies a reasoned standard consistently while examining cultural context
Ignores consent and harm
Assumes one culture is always superior
Treats every custom as identical
quizQuestions.answer: Applies a reasoned standard consistently while examining cultural context
quizQuestions.explanation: Universalism need not erase context; it asks whether a defensible principle applies consistently across cases.

quizQuestions.question: In Logic & Argument Structure, An argument is VALID if:
options: Its premises are all factually true
Both its premises and conclusion are true
It uses formal logical notation and symbols
Its conclusion follows necessarily from its premises, regardless of whether the premises are true
quizQuestions.answer: Its conclusion follows necessarily from its premises, regardless of whether the premises are true
quizQuestions.explanation: Validity is a structural property: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true. An argument can be valid even with false premises.

quizQuestions.question: An argument is SOUND if it is:
options: Rhetorically effective regardless of logical structure
Valid and likely to persuade its audience
Inductive and supported by statistical evidence
Valid AND all of its premises are actually true
quizQuestions.answer: Valid AND all of its premises are actually true
quizQuestions.explanation: A sound argument is both valid (conclusion follows from premises) and has premises that are actually true — soundness guarantees that the conclusion is also true.

quizQuestions.question: Consider: All birds are mammals; all robins are birds; therefore all robins are mammals. How should this argument be classified?
options: Invalid because the conclusion is false
Valid but unsound because its form works while a premise is false
Inductive because it discusses animals
Sound because robins are birds
quizQuestions.answer: Valid but unsound because its form works while a premise is false
quizQuestions.explanation: The syllogistic form is valid, but the premise that all birds are mammals is false, so the argument is not sound.

quizQuestions.question: What is the best way to show that a deductive argument form is invalid?
options: Give a counterexample with true premises and a false conclusion
Count how many people accept it
Disagree with its topic
Replace its conclusion with a question
quizQuestions.answer: Give a counterexample with true premises and a false conclusion
quizQuestions.explanation: One possible case with true premises and a false conclusion proves that the conclusion does not follow necessarily.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: State one valid deductive argument form and give a one-sentence example.
quizQuestions.answer: Example: Modus ponens — If a source is independently verified, it passes this check; Source A is independently verified; therefore Source A passes this check.
quizQuestions.explanation: A correct response names a valid form such as modus ponens, modus tollens, or a valid syllogism and instantiates it so a true-premise case could not have a false conclusion.

quizQuestions.question: An ad hominem fallacy occurs when someone:
options: Makes an appeal to human emotions to win an argument
Attacks the character or identity of the arguer rather than the argument itself
Uses examples that are too specific to support a general conclusion
Attacks the argument by showing its premises are false
quizQuestions.answer: Attacks the character or identity of the arguer rather than the argument itself
quizQuestions.explanation: Ad hominem attacks the person making an argument (their credibility, character, or circumstances) rather than addressing the argument's logic or evidence.

quizQuestions.question: The straw man fallacy involves:
options: Misrepresenting an opponent's argument to make it easier to attack
Assuming the conclusion in one of the premises of an argument
Using weak examples to support a strong conclusion
Appealing to the authority of a famous person to win a debate
quizQuestions.answer: Misrepresenting an opponent's argument to make it easier to attack
quizQuestions.explanation: The straw man fallacy distorts or exaggerates an opponent's position into a weaker version, then attacks that distorted version rather than the actual argument.

quizQuestions.question: An argument says, 'Mina proposes one car-free street, so she wants to ban every vehicle.' Which fallacy is this?
options: Straw man
Appeal to expertise
Valid deduction
False cause
quizQuestions.answer: Straw man
quizQuestions.explanation: The response exaggerates Mina's limited proposal into an easier extreme position to attack.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Complete this statement: An appeal to authority is fallacious when...
quizQuestions.answer: An appeal to authority is fallacious when the authority lacks relevant expertise, is misrepresented, is used in place of evidence, or is treated as beyond reasonable challenge.
quizQuestions.explanation: Expert testimony can be useful, but it becomes weak reasoning when expertise, evidence, and context are ignored.

quizQuestions.question: In evaluating evidence, anecdotal evidence is generally considered weaker than statistical evidence because:
options: A single case cannot reliably represent a larger pattern across many cases
Statistics are always collected by more reliable researchers than personal stories
Statistics are easier to understand than personal narratives
Anecdotes are always intentionally fabricated to mislead
quizQuestions.answer: A single case cannot reliably represent a larger pattern across many cases
quizQuestions.explanation: Anecdotal evidence (individual stories or cases) cannot reliably generalize — one person's experience may be exceptional and not representative of the broader pattern.

quizQuestions.question: Confirmation bias in evaluating evidence is the tendency to:
options: Wait for confirmation from government authorities before accepting any claim
Accept only evidence from sources that require confirmation from multiple experts
Seek, interpret, and remember information that confirms existing beliefs while dismissing contradicting evidence
Always confirm the majority view before forming a personal opinion
quizQuestions.answer: Seek, interpret, and remember information that confirms existing beliefs while dismissing contradicting evidence
quizQuestions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the cognitive tendency to favor evidence that supports pre-existing beliefs and to discount, avoid, or reinterpret evidence that contradicts them.

quizQuestions.question: Correlation does not imply causation means that:
options: Correlated variables can never be causally related
Only randomized controlled experiments can identify correlated variables
Statistical analysis cannot reveal relationships between variables
Two variables that consistently vary together may not have a cause-and-effect relationship
quizQuestions.answer: Two variables that consistently vary together may not have a cause-and-effect relationship
quizQuestions.explanation: Correlation shows that two variables move together but does not prove that one causes the other — a third variable may cause both, or the correlation may be coincidental.

quizQuestions.question: After seeing a viral claim, which action best follows the SIFT method?
options: Pause and trace the claim to its original context before sharing
Assume a professional design guarantees accuracy
Read only the headline
Count likes as proof
quizQuestions.answer: Pause and trace the claim to its original context before sharing
quizQuestions.explanation: SIFT begins by stopping and then investigating the source, finding better coverage, and tracing the claim to its origin.

questions.question: The fundamental question that normative ethics attempts to answer is:
options: What actions, practices, or values are morally right or good?
How do people actually behave in moral situations?
How can we scientifically measure the morality of actions?
What is the historical origin of our moral beliefs?
questions.answer: What actions, practices, or values are morally right or good?
questions.explanation: Normative ethics is prescriptive — it asks what we ought to do, what is good, and what principles should guide moral decisions.

questions.question: A relief plan helps 30 people by 3 utility points each, while another helps 80 people by 1 point each and has no other effects. Under the supplied act-utilitarian model, which plan is preferred?
options: The 80-person plan because it reaches more people regardless of total utility
The plan favored by the decision-maker
Neither, because utilitarianism never compares quantities
The 30-person plan because its total utility is 90
questions.answer: The 30-person plan because its total utility is 90
questions.explanation: The supplied model compares total consequences: 30×3 = 90, which exceeds 80×1 = 80.

questions.question: A person adopts the maxim “I will never help anyone, even when aid is easy and safe.” Kant’s universal-law analysis most directly criticizes this maxim because:
options: A rational person could not consistently will a world with no mutual aid while recognizing that anyone may sometimes need help
The maxim is illegal in every society
The maxim attacks the character of anyone requesting help
The maxim always produces the smallest total happiness
questions.answer: A rational person could not consistently will a world with no mutual aid while recognizing that anyone may sometimes need help
questions.explanation: The maxim illustrates a contradiction in will and supports an imperfect duty of beneficence: rational agents can recognize that they may need others’ help while pursuing their own ends.

questions.question: A team leader regularly invites criticism, admits mistakes, and changes course after careful deliberation. In virtue ethics, this pattern most clearly shows:
options: A calculation that ignores character
Moral luck alone
A stable character disposition shaped through practice
A single rule followed without judgment
questions.answer: A stable character disposition shaped through practice
questions.explanation: Virtue ethics evaluates cultivated dispositions expressed consistently and guided by practical wisdom, not one isolated act.

questions.question: A common objection to culture-relative moral truth is that it can make which claim difficult to justify?
options: The descriptive claim that cultures sometimes disagree
The claim that context matters when interpreting conduct
A culture-independent condemnation of a practice accepted within another culture
The claim that people can learn other moral traditions
questions.answer: A culture-independent condemnation of a practice accepted within another culture
questions.explanation: The objection concerns the lack of a culture-independent standard; a relativist may still condemn a practice from within the evaluator’s own framework.

questions.question: All registered voters may enter the forum. Leila is a registered voter. Therefore Leila may enter the forum. If both premises are true, the argument is:
options: Inductive because it applies a general rule
Sound because it is valid and has true premises
Invalid because the conclusion concerns permission
Valid but unsound because its conclusion is true
questions.answer: Sound because it is valid and has true premises
questions.explanation: The conclusion follows deductively from the premises, and the prompt states that the premises are true.

questions.question: During a debate, Kai answers a safety study by saying, “Ignore it; the researcher is annoying.” Which error is Kai making?
questions.answer: Kai commits an ad hominem fallacy by attacking the researcher rather than addressing the study’s evidence or reasoning.
questions.explanation: A complete answer identifies the personal attack and explains that it does not answer the claim.

questions.question: A buyer reads only reviews that praise a product and dismisses equally credible negative tests without checking them. This best illustrates:
options: A valid counterexample
Confirmation bias
The doctrine of the mean
Proportionate sampling
questions.answer: Confirmation bias
questions.explanation: The buyer selectively seeks and evaluates evidence in ways that support an existing preference.

questions.question: A manager hides a defect report so customers will keep buying a product. Under Kant's Formula of Humanity, the central problem is that the manager:
options: Breaks a cultural custom but no duty
Uses customers merely as a means by denying information needed for rational choice
Fails to maximize quarterly profit
Chooses an action with uncertain consequences
questions.answer: Uses customers merely as a means by denying information needed for rational choice
questions.explanation: Deception manipulates customers' decisions and prevents them from acting as informed rational agents.

questions.question: A normally courageous person rushes into danger without assessing whether help is useful. Aristotle would most likely describe the action as:
options: Proof that consequences alone determine virtue
A deficiency of generosity
An excess approaching recklessness
The exact mean in every circumstance
questions.answer: An excess approaching recklessness
questions.explanation: The doctrine of the mean treats courage as an appropriate response between cowardice and reckless excess, guided by practical wisdom.

questions.question: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights reflects which moral approach?
options: Virtue ethics — rights earned through virtuous conduct
Moral relativism — different standards for different cultures
Rule utilitarianism — rights that generally maximize welfare
Moral universalism — rights that apply to all humans everywhere
questions.answer: Moral universalism — rights that apply to all humans everywhere
questions.explanation: The UDHR is grounded in moral universalism — the belief that all humans possess certain rights by virtue of their humanity, which no cultural or state authority can legitimately override.

questions.question: A town installs new lights on Monday; reported theft falls on Tuesday. A council member concludes the lights caused the change without considering other evidence. Which fallacy is present?
options: Appeal to irrelevant authority
Post hoc reasoning
Valid modus ponens
Straw man
questions.answer: Post hoc reasoning
questions.explanation: Temporal sequence alone does not establish causation; alternative causes and longer-term evidence are needed.

questions.question: One family reports success with a tutoring app. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The testimonial shows one experience but cannot establish the app’s typical effect
The app caused the result because the report is sincere
No further evidence could change the conclusion
The app improves scores for all students
questions.answer: The testimonial shows one experience but cannot establish the app’s typical effect
questions.explanation: Anecdotal evidence can describe a case but cannot reliably estimate a broader causal effect.

questions.question: A student says, “If one deadline extension is allowed, soon no deadlines will matter and the entire course will collapse,” without supporting the chain of events. Name the fallacy and explain it briefly.
questions.answer: This is a slippery-slope fallacy: it asserts an escalating chain from one extension to course collapse without evidence for the intermediate steps.
questions.explanation: A complete answer identifies the unsupported causal chain rather than treating the first decision as proof of every later outcome.

questions.question: Mill's modification to Bentham's utilitarianism distinguished between 'higher' and 'lower' pleasures because he argued that:
options: Only pleasures that society approves should be counted
Intellectual and moral pleasures are qualitatively superior to physical pleasures
The intensity of pleasure is the only morally relevant factor
Rich people's pleasures should count more in utilitarian calculations
questions.answer: Intellectual and moral pleasures are qualitatively superior to physical pleasures
questions.explanation: Mill argued that not all pleasures are equal in quality — intellectual, artistic, and moral pleasures are qualitatively superior to mere physical satisfaction, even at lower intensity.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: Rule utilitarianism differs from act utilitarianism by evaluating actions based on:
options: The expected consequences of following a general rule
An argument that attacks a person instead of a claim
The actual consequences of the specific action
A conclusion chosen before considering evidence
questions.answer: The expected consequences of following a general rule
questions.explanation: The best answer is "The expected consequences of following a general rule" because it directly addresses the concept being assessed.

questions.question: A student considers using a rule, “I may make false promises whenever doing so is convenient.” Under the Formula of Universal Law, the central problem is that:
options: The rule is acceptable whenever the student feels sincere
Universalization asks only whether the rule is legal
The rule is wrong only if someone is immediately harmed
Universalizing the rule would undermine the practice of promising that the maxim depends on
questions.answer: Universalizing the rule would undermine the practice of promising that the maxim depends on
questions.explanation: If false promising were a universal permission, people could not rationally rely on promises, creating a contradiction in conception.

questions.question: Virtue ethics focuses on the development of character over time primarily because:
options: Rules and consequences are never reliable guides to action
Being a good person with good character naturally leads to right actions across diverse situations
Virtuous character is inherited rather than developed
Character determines legal standing in civil and criminal courts
questions.answer: Being a good person with good character naturally leads to right actions across diverse situations
questions.explanation: Virtue ethics holds that rules and calculations are insufficient — a person of good character (courageous, honest, just) will perceive what situations require and respond appropriately.

questions.question: A policy creates a modest total benefit but imposes a severe avoidable burden on one uninformed person. Which question most directly adds a rights-based check to a utility calculation?
options: Can every effect be expressed in dollars?
Is the policy popular with the largest group?
Does the policy produce any benefit at all?
Does the policy respect that person’s agency and basic claims?
questions.answer: Does the policy respect that person’s agency and basic claims?
questions.explanation: A rights-based analysis asks whether individuals are treated with due respect rather than only aggregating total welfare.

questions.question: A rule against concealing known safety defects sometimes reduces short-term profit but generally prevents harm and supports trust. A rule utilitarian would assess it mainly by:
options: Whether the rule appears in every legal code
Whether one concealment happens to increase profit
The expected consequences of general acceptance of the rule
The personality of one manager
questions.answer: The expected consequences of general acceptance of the rule
questions.explanation: Rule utilitarianism evaluates the consequences of a generally followed rule rather than only one isolated act.

questions.question: Short response: Explain the difference between a valid argument and a sound argument, and give one brief example.
questions.answer: A valid argument has a form in which true premises could not lead to a false conclusion; a sound argument is valid and also has true premises. Example: All mammals are warm-blooded; whales are mammals; therefore whales are warm-blooded.
questions.explanation: A complete answer states both conditions and supplies an example whose structure and premises support the classification.

questions.question: A normally cautious student refuses every reasonable opportunity to speak, even after preparation. In Aristotelian terms, this response most likely shows:
options: An excess of courage
A deficiency relative to the courageous mean
A utilitarian calculation
The ideal mean because caution is always virtuous
questions.answer: A deficiency relative to the courageous mean
questions.explanation: The doctrine of the mean treats virtue as context-sensitive; too little confidence can be a deficiency just as recklessness can be an excess.

questions.question: Two sources make the same causal claim. One reports a comparison group, attrition, and uncertainty; the other quotes a sponsor and links no study. Which is the strongest reason to prefer the first source?
options: It uses more confident language
It agrees with the claim first encountered
Its method and limitations are more traceable and independently assessable
It guarantees that its conclusion is true
questions.answer: Its method and limitations are more traceable and independently assessable
questions.explanation: Traceable methods, comparison data, and disclosed uncertainty permit stronger evaluation; they do not guarantee truth.

questions.question: Why can applying both consequence-based and duty-based reasoning improve analysis of a difficult case?
options: It guarantees that all frameworks reach the same verdict
It removes the need to identify stakeholders
It permits choosing any preferred answer without justification
It reveals effects and constraints that either framework alone might miss
questions.answer: It reveals effects and constraints that either framework alone might miss
questions.explanation: Using multiple frameworks can expose welfare effects, duties, rights, and tradeoffs that require explicit justification.

questions.question: An employee discovers that a product report omits a serious risk. Before recommending disclosure, which analysis is most complete?
options: Count only the employee’s personal cost
Share the allegation publicly before checking the evidence
Identify duties, likely harms, affected stakeholders, evidence quality, and safer reporting channels
Assume disclosure is always wrong because loyalty is absolute
questions.answer: Identify duties, likely harms, affected stakeholders, evidence quality, and safer reporting channels
questions.explanation: A defensible recommendation considers duties, consequences, stakeholders, evidence, and proportionate ways to reduce harm.

questions.question: A study praising a tutoring product was funded by its vendor. What is the best response?
options: Accept the study because sponsorship guarantees access to data
Treat funding as a reason to inspect methods and corroboration, not as automatic proof of error
Reject the study solely because funding exists
Ignore funding and read only the conclusion
questions.answer: Treat funding as a reason to inspect methods and corroboration, not as automatic proof of error
questions.explanation: A conflict of interest can raise risk of bias, but the evidence still requires examination rather than automatic acceptance or rejection.

questions.question: The correlation-causation distinction is important in ethical reasoning because:
options: Only causal evidence is admissible in ethical arguments
Correlations are always statistically stronger than causal relationships
Correlational research is conducted by less credible researchers
Mistaking correlation for causation can lead to ineffective or harmful policy interventions
questions.answer: Mistaking correlation for causation can lead to ineffective or harmful policy interventions
questions.explanation: Misidentifying a correlation as causal leads to wrong solutions — targeting the symptom rather than the cause, wasting resources, and potentially causing harm through misguided intervention.

questions.question: The false dilemma fallacy is problematic in ethical reasoning because it:
questions.answer: The false dilemma fallacy is problematic because it reduces a complex ethical issue to only two choices and ignores alternatives, nuance, or compromise.
questions.explanation: Ethical reasoning often requires weighing several values, so artificial either-or framing can hide better or more responsible options.

questions.question: Which practice most directly reduces confirmation bias during a source review?
options: Stop after finding one supporting example
Write decision criteria first and actively seek credible disconfirming evidence
Rate a claim by how often it appears in a feed
Read only sources that use familiar terminology
questions.answer: Write decision criteria first and actively seek credible disconfirming evidence
questions.explanation: Precommitted criteria and deliberate search for credible counterevidence make selective evaluation less likely.

questions.question: In the argument “If the evidence is independently replicated, confidence should rise; the evidence was independently replicated; therefore confidence should rise,” which statement is the conclusion?
options: Independent replication is impossible
Confidence should rise
The evidence was independently replicated
If the evidence is independently replicated, confidence should rise
questions.answer: Confidence should rise
questions.explanation: The conclusion is the claim supported by the conditional premise and the stated antecedent.

questions.question: Moral intuitions are best treated in ethical reasoning as:
options: Irrelevant subjective feelings that ethical reasoning must eliminate
Direct windows into objective moral truth that require no further analysis
Absolute moral truths that override all theoretical arguments
Significant data points that should be taken seriously but subjected to critical reflection
questions.answer: Significant data points that should be taken seriously but subjected to critical reflection
questions.explanation: Strong moral intuitions carry evidential weight — they reflect accumulated moral experience — but they can also reflect bias, culture, or limited perspective, requiring critical reflection.

questions.question: A community practice is disputed across cultures. Which statement best distinguishes description from justification?
options: Any disagreement proves every moral claim is false
Showing that standards differ describes disagreement; it does not by itself prove that no cross-cultural standard is justified
Cultural context is irrelevant to ethical judgment
A universal claim never needs reasons
questions.answer: Showing that standards differ describes disagreement; it does not by itself prove that no cross-cultural standard is justified
questions.explanation: The existence of disagreement is a descriptive fact and does not logically settle the metaethical question.

questions.question: Evidence suggests a benefit, but the estimate has a wide uncertainty interval and substantial attrition. Which conclusion is best?
options: Uncertainty can be ignored when a result is favorable
The benefit is certain because the point estimate is positive
The result is suggestive, but confidence should remain limited until stronger evidence is available
The study proves there is no benefit
questions.answer: The result is suggestive, but confidence should remain limited until stronger evidence is available
questions.explanation: A bounded conclusion reflects the direction of the evidence while acknowledging imprecision and possible attrition bias.

questions.question: After encountering a viral claim, which sequence best applies SIFT?
options: Judge the claim from the headline and follower count
Share first, then look for confirming comments
Stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, and trace the claim to its original context
Read only the page that made the claim
questions.answer: Stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, and trace the claim to its original context
questions.explanation: SIFT starts by pausing before reacting, then checks the source’s reputation, looks laterally for stronger independent coverage, and traces quotations, images, or claims back to their original context before accepting or sharing them.

questions.question: Explain one important difference between law and ethics, then give a fictional example of conduct that could be legal but ethically questionable.
questions.answer: Law sets enforceable public rules, while ethics asks what is morally justified or responsible. Example: a company may legally retain more customer data than needed, yet the practice may be ethically questionable because it increases privacy risk without sufficient benefit.
questions.explanation: A complete answer states the distinct roles of law and ethics and applies the distinction to a plausible case.
